To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the trellis complexity of a linear code is a monotonic function of the code length and the code dimension and is minimized for the cyclic code (or the shortened cyclic code) or its extended code of the same length.

the complexity of a minimal trelis diagram for a linear code of length n and dimension k is bounded by 2/sup k/ times a polynomial function of n and the number of states is minimized for a cyclic (or extended cyclic) code of the same length, dimension and minimum distance.

the complexity of the minimal-state trellis diagram of a linear block code depends only on its length and dimension; the worst linear block code in terms of the complexity of its minimal-state trellises is the cyclic or shortened cyclic code or its extended version; and the minimal-state trelli diagram for a linear code of length 2/m/ is of order 4/m/.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the complexity of the trellis diagrams of linear block codes is determined by the number of information bits and by the minimum distance of the code.
the complexity of trellises for linear codes is closely related to the complexity of their generator matrices.
the complexity of the trellis structure for linear codes is closely related to the complexity of the algebraic structure of the code.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, for the same length and minimum distance, the extended BCH code and its permuted version have a smaller number of trellis states than the original BCH code in the cyclic form.
, in general, the trellis complexity of a code can be significantly reduced by using a bit-position permutation and an appropriate extension of the code.
the trellis state-complexity of linear codes is not an intrinsic property of codes but depends on their representation in a trellis diagram.
